 Even with SNAP benefits, getting enough food in Mass. can be difficult

 Even with SNAP benefits, getting enough food in Mass. can be difficult 
 Share
 Email

 Nurjhan Greenidge searches for deals to help make her SNAP benefits go farther 
 Craig LeMoult
 GBH News
 Craig LeMoult
 clemoult 
 Craig LeMoult is a reporter for GBH News. Feedback? Questions? Story ideas? Reach out to Craig at craig.lemoult@gbh.org. 
 November 18, 2026
 “Today’s my food stamp day,” Nurjhan Greenidge said as she walked along crowded sidewalks from her North End apartment. “So today we’re going grocery shopping. So we get to see what my $110 does.”
 That’s how much Greenidge gets each month from the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. Greenidge lives off Social Security disability benefits.
 “Once I paid all my bills, I still owe $200,” she said. “I come in arrears every month, so I’m living off of credit cards, like everybody else.”

 Become a GBH sponsor 
 That means the monthly help from SNAP is crucial.
 “If I didn’t have SNAP, I wouldn’t be eating,” she said. “Like today. I wouldn’t be eating today.”
 For many Massachusetts families, that help has disappeared. Since the Trump administration put new limits on eligibility in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, nearly 200,000 people in Massachusetts have lost their SNAP benefits, including 70,000 children, according to the advocacy group Project Bread.
 Greenidge said a neighbor of hers is among those who lost benefits.
 “They wanted her to go to work, but she’s on disability, and she could never get in contact with anybody,” she said. “So her food stamps were cut. So she survives off of the food pantry.”
 Greenidge arrives at the grocery store with a mission: “Our goal today is to spend $40, so that way we can stretch the food stamps for four weeks,” she said.

 She headed straight to the pile of circulars just inside. They advertised deals on eggs and tomato sauce.
 “As long as we stick to the list, we should be fine,” she said as she began shopping.
 Greenidge navigated her shopping cart through the aisles and stopped by the refrigerated case of ground meat.
 “Even if I bought ground chicken, $5.49, it’s very expensive. Wow,” she said. “Yeah, we’re gonna hold off on that.”
 A couple containers of sliced fruit, some pasta and some cranberry juice went in the cart, and there was a special on canned beans and tomatoes.
 Nurjhan Greenidge finds a deal on canned beans 
 Craig LeMoult
 GBH News
 At the register, as the items were rung up, she waited to see if she managed to stay within her $40 budget.
 This is a suspense that’s all too familiar around the state as families face growing food insecurity. A report released in April by the Greater Boston Food Bank said at some point over the last year, 40% of households in the state either couldn’t afford enough food or worried about where their next meal would come from. Even those who haven’t lost SNAP benefits are struggling.
 “Benefits, even though you get [it] monthly, really covers about two weeks worth of groceries,” said Leran Minc of Project Bread.
 Stretching out those benefits becomes more challenging with food prices jumping nearly 30% in the last six years.
 “Food is often the first thing people cut when they’re financially struggling,” Minc said.
 Housing, transportation and medical expenses often take precedence, he added. During the pandemic, Minc said, food insecurity fell across the country because of policies expanding access to SNAP, and increasing how much money people got.
 “And those policy choices have now shifted to weakening the program, kicking people off of a program, and really making it all more complicated,” Minc said. “And so it’s really hard to hear — and it’s something we hear often — about how people continue to struggle, even if they get benefits.”
 At the register, Greenidge chose not to get a couple bags of tortilla chips that she’d mistakenly thought were on sale. That put her close to her goal: The total was $41.25.
 “My main objective today was to get protein, so the beans are protein, because the meat was too expensive,” she said, adding that she’ll keep looking for a sale on meat, or she’ll see what she can get at a food pantry.
 As she walked back home, Greenidge glanced in the grocery bags and thought about the week ahead.
 “I mean, even though I’ve got stuff on sale, the bags are still kind of empty,” she said.
